sentences.text: Lufengosaurus is often described as a small early sauropodomorph approximately 6 meters long.
This animal possessed a deep, broad snout featuring distinctive bony bumps located behind its nostrils and on its cheeks.
Its mouth contained closely spaced, serrated teeth specifically suited for a diet based on leaves.
When including larger specimens, the creature measured approximately 6 meters in length and nearly 3 meters in height.
The first remains were discovered in the late 1930s by geologist Bien Meinian in the Lower Lufeng Formation near Lufeng, Yunnan Province, China.
C. C. Young named the type species Lufengosaurus huenei in 1940, deriving the genus name from the location Lufeng and the species name from his mentor Friedrich von Huene.
A second species, Lufengosaurus magnus, was named by Young in 1940 and fully described in 1947.
Researchers inferred that Lufengosaurus was bipedal based on its long neck and relatively short forelimbs.
Lufengosaurus was herbivorous despite possessing sharp claws, including a large thumb claw.
It is thought that Lufengosaurus used its thumb claw for defense or to strip leaves from trees.
Young originally assigned Lufengosaurus to the family Plateosauridae within the suborder Prosauropoda.
While sometimes considered a member of Plateosauridae, some cladistic analyses classify Lufengosaurus as a member of Massospondylidae.
Lufengosaurus was a massospondylid dinosaur that lived in southwestern China during the Early Jurassic period.
Lufengosaurus lived approximately 203 to 191 million years ago during the Hettangian and Pliensbachian stages of the Early Jurassic in what is now Asia.
It is debated whether Lufengosaurus was partially omnivorous based on its sharp claws and teeth, though its teeth resemble those of herbivorous iguanian lizards.
In the West, Lufengosaurus magnus is often considered a modern synonym of Lufengosaurus huenei, representing large individuals.
However, the identity of Gyposaurus sinensis as Lufengosaurus is generally doubted today.
In 1981, Michael Cooper suggested that Lufengosaurus and Yunnanosaurus were species of the South African genus Massospondylus.
